sources.title: Preparing Your Older Child for a New Baby: How to Help Siblings Adjust
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 2/10/2026)
sources.quote: Expect your child to regress a little. For example, your toilet-trained child might suddenly start having "accidents," or they might want to take a bottle. This is normal and is your older child's way of making sure they still have your love and attention. Instead of telling them to act their age, let him have the attention they need. Praise them when they act more grown-up. ... Set aside special time for your child. ... play games, listen to music or simply talk together. ... Find ways to invite your child to help. You want to make sure your child feels included and not excluded. This helps build a bond between siblings, reduce jealousy and promote curiosity. ... Remind your child about when they were a baby. Show your child their baby pictures. ... Explain to your child that sometimes you need to take care of baby first. ... Make an effort to spend some time alone with them each day. ... Read children's books about newborns and siblings with your child.
sources.supports: Regression is normal and not to be answered with act your age, praise for grown-up behaviour, special one on one time each day, inviting the child to help, baby pictures, explaining that baby sometimes comes first, and reading books about siblings. An American Academy of Pediatrics page applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts)
sources.quote: All this change can be hard for older siblings to handle. It's common for them to feel jealousy toward the newborn and to act out. ... Many kids want to help take care of a new baby. Though that "help" may mean that each task takes longer, it can give an older child a chance to interact with the baby in a positive way. ... Take advantage of chances for one-on-one time with older kids. Spend time together while the baby is sleeping and, if possible, set aside time each day for older kids to get one parent's undivided attention. ... Also remind relatives and friends that your older child might want to talk about something other than the new baby. ... If your child acts up, don't bend the rules, but understand what feelings may be motivating that behavior.
sources.supports: Jealousy and acting out are common, kids often want to help, daily one on one time, relatives asking about something other than the baby, and understanding the feeling behind the behaviour. A Nemours KidsHealth page applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: Preparing Your Older Child for a New Baby: How to Help Siblings Adjust
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 2/10/2026)
sources.quote: Expect your child to regress a little. For example, your toilet-trained child might suddenly start having "accidents," or they might want to take a bottle. This is normal and is your older child's way of making sure they still have your love and attention. Instead of telling them to act their age, let him have the attention they need. Praise them when they act more grown-up. ... Set aside special time for your child. ... play games, listen to music or simply talk together. ... Find ways to invite your child to help. You want to make sure your child feels included and not excluded. This helps build a bond between siblings, reduce jealousy and promote curiosity. ... Remind your child about when they were a baby. Show your child their baby pictures. ... Explain to your child that sometimes you need to take care of baby first. ... Make an effort to spend some time alone with them each day. ... Read children's books about newborns and siblings with your child.
sources.supports: Regression is normal and not to be answered with act your age, praise for grown-up behaviour, special one on one time each day, inviting the child to help, baby pictures, explaining that baby sometimes comes first, and reading books about siblings. An American Academy of Pediatrics page applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts)
sources.quote: All this change can be hard for older siblings to handle. It's common for them to feel jealousy toward the newborn and to act out. ... Many kids want to help take care of a new baby. Though that "help" may mean that each task takes longer, it can give an older child a chance to interact with the baby in a positive way. ... Take advantage of chances for one-on-one time with older kids. Spend time together while the baby is sleeping and, if possible, set aside time each day for older kids to get one parent's undivided attention. ... Also remind relatives and friends that your older child might want to talk about something other than the new baby. ... If your child acts up, don't bend the rules, but understand what feelings may be motivating that behavior.
sources.supports: Jealousy and acting out are common, kids often want to help, daily one on one time, relatives asking about something other than the baby, and understanding the feeling behind the behaviour. A Nemours KidsHealth page applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: Preparing Your Older Child for a New Baby: How to Help Siblings Adjust
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 2/10/2026)
sources.quote: Expect your child to regress a little. For example, your toilet-trained child might suddenly start having "accidents," or they might want to take a bottle. This is normal and is your older child's way of making sure they still have your love and attention. Instead of telling them to act their age, let him have the attention they need. Praise them when they act more grown-up. ... Set aside special time for your child. ... play games, listen to music or simply talk together. ... Find ways to invite your child to help. You want to make sure your child feels included and not excluded. This helps build a bond between siblings, reduce jealousy and promote curiosity. ... Remind your child about when they were a baby. Show your child their baby pictures. ... Explain to your child that sometimes you need to take care of baby first. ... Make an effort to spend some time alone with them each day. ... Read children's books about newborns and siblings with your child.
sources.supports: Regression is normal and not to be answered with act your age, praise for grown-up behaviour, special one on one time each day, inviting the child to help, baby pictures, explaining that baby sometimes comes first, and reading books about siblings. An American Academy of Pediatrics page applied to Israeli families as general child health advice.

sources.title: Preparing Your Child for a New Sibling
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts)
sources.quote: All this change can be hard for older siblings to handle. It's common for them to feel jealousy toward the newborn and to act out. ... Many kids want to help take care of a new baby. Though that "help" may mean that each task takes longer, it can give an older child a chance to interact with the baby in a positive way. ... Take advantage of chances for one-on-one time with older kids. Spend time together while the baby is sleeping and, if possible, set aside time each day for older kids to get one parent's undivided attention. ... Also remind relatives and friends that your older child might want to talk about something other than the new baby. ... If your child acts up, don't bend the rules, but understand what feelings may be motivating that behavior.
sources.supports: Jealousy and acting out are common, kids often want to help, daily one on one time, relatives asking about something other than the baby, and understanding the feeling behind the behaviour. A Nemours KidsHealth page applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: Language Development: 1 Year Olds
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (from Caring for Your Baby and Young Child, 2009)
sources.quote: Early in the second year, your toddler will suddenly seem to understand everything you say. ... Most toddlers master at least fifty spoken words by the end of the second year and can put two words together to form a short sentence, although there are differences among children. ... By all means, don’t ridicule his language mistakes. Give him as much time as he needs to finish what he wants to say without hurrying, and then answer with a correct pronunciation of the word (“That’s right, it’s a ball!”). ... He might point and say “ball”—his way of telling you he wants you to roll him the ball.
sources.supports: Toddlers seem to understand more than they say, differences among children, giving time, answering with the correct word without ridicule, and pointing with a single word as an early sentence. An American Academy of Pediatrics page (2009) applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: First words and little sentences: 1 to 2 years
sources.quote: Chatting about your daily routine, like getting dressed, is a great way for your child to hear the same words every day. ... Look at picture books together ... give your child time to point things out and talk about what they can see ... Name objects and offer your child choices, for example, "Do you want an apple or an orange?". ... Explore fun songs and rhymes with actions and props. Singing together is a great way to connect! ... Remember, children learn to talk at different ages. If you are worried, speak to your health visitor or nursery key worker
sources.supports: Talking through routines such as getting dressed, picture books and time to point, offering choices, songs with actions, and that children learn to talk at different ages. An NHS page for English families applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: Language Development: 1 Year Olds
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (from Caring for Your Baby and Young Child, 2009)
sources.quote: Early in the second year, your toddler will suddenly seem to understand everything you say. ... Most toddlers master at least fifty spoken words by the end of the second year and can put two words together to form a short sentence, although there are differences among children. ... By all means, don’t ridicule his language mistakes. Give him as much time as he needs to finish what he wants to say without hurrying, and then answer with a correct pronunciation of the word (“That’s right, it’s a ball!”). ... He might point and say “ball”—his way of telling you he wants you to roll him the ball.
sources.supports: Toddlers seem to understand more than they say, differences among children, giving time, answering with the correct word without ridicule, and pointing with a single word as an early sentence. An American Academy of Pediatrics page (2009) applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: First words and little sentences: 1 to 2 years
sources.quote: Chatting about your daily routine, like getting dressed, is a great way for your child to hear the same words every day. ... Look at picture books together ... give your child time to point things out and talk about what they can see ... Name objects and offer your child choices, for example, "Do you want an apple or an orange?". ... Explore fun songs and rhymes with actions and props. Singing together is a great way to connect! ... Remember, children learn to talk at different ages. If you are worried, speak to your health visitor or nursery key worker
sources.supports: Talking through routines such as getting dressed, picture books and time to point, offering choices, songs with actions, and that children learn to talk at different ages. An NHS page for English families applied to Israeli families as general advice.

ביום שלישי, בגינה, יצאה לי מילה.
אתם קפצתם ממקום.
> ״כן, שירה, זה כדור! כדור גדול!״
ואז אמרתי אותה **שוב**.

scene.action: In the garden the girl holds a red ball up high with a stunned happy face while her parents jump up from a bench with delighted smiles.
scene.setting: A small Israeli neighbourhood garden in the afternoon with a low hedge, a plain pale warm sky above. The upper third of the frame stays calm: a plain soft background, no faces or hands there.

slides.label: ומאז
slides.headline: אתם מדברים, אני שומעת
slides.body:
## מה יעזור לי:
שתגידו מה אתם עושים, בקול רגוע:
״עכשיו מלבישים, יד אחת, יד שנייה.״
אותן מילים, כל יום, ואני **אוספת** אותן.

scene.action: The mother helps the girl into a sweater in the bedroom, talking calmly and smiling, while the girl looks at her face.
scene.setting: A cosy Israeli child bedroom: a low wooden bed, a plain warm cream wall, a small night light on a shelf, soft evening light. The upper third of the frame stays calm: a plain soft background, no faces or hands there.

slides.label: ומאז
slides.headline: ספר עם תמונות, כל ערב
slides.body:
אני מצביעה, ואתם אומרים מה זה.
״כלב.״ ״ציפור.״ ״אדום.״
ואני מנסה להגיד אחריכם.
אין לחץ, זה **משחק**.

scene.action: The girl sits between her parents on the bed in the evening pointing at an animal picture in a big book while the father reads.
scene.setting: A cosy Israeli child bedroom: a low wooden bed, a plain warm cream wall, a small night light on a shelf, soft evening light. The upper third of the frame stays calm: a plain soft background, no faces or hands there.

slides.label: ומאז
slides.headline: אתם מחכים שאסיים
slides.body:
לפעמים אני אומרת ״כ...״ ועוצרת.
אתם לא ממהרים להשלים.
אתם מחכים, ואז עונים נכון:
> ״כן, זה כדור!״

scene.action: The girl reaches toward a ball with a concentrating expression while her father waits beside her with a patient smile.
scene.setting: The family's Israeli living room: a beige sofa, a soft rug, a plain warm cream wall, warm soft light. The upper third of the frame stays calm: a plain soft background, no faces or hands there.

slides.label: מה שמחזיר לי את פעם
slides.headline: כשאני עייפה, אני מצביעה
slides.body:
וזה בסדר גמור.
## מה יעזור לי:
שתגידו את המילה בשבילי,
בלי ״תגידי!״ בלי סוף.
ומחר אני מנסה **שוב**.

scene.action: The tired girl rubs her eyes in her mother's arms on the sofa and points weakly at a cup while her mother smiles and names it.
scene.setting: The family's Israeli living room: a beige sofa, a soft rug, a plain warm cream wall, warm soft light. The upper third of the frame stays calm: a plain soft background, no faces or hands there.

slides.headline: אני מדברת בקצב שלי
slides.body:
בשבילכם זו מילה אחת, ״כדור״.
בשבילי זה הר שטיפסתי עליו.
אז תמשיכו לדבר איתי, לשיר ולחכות.
אני **בדרך**.

scene.action: The girl stands in the garden between her parents holding both their hands and the red ball under one arm, all of them smiling.
scene.setting: A small Israeli neighbourhood garden in the afternoon with a low hedge, a plain pale warm sky above. The upper third of the frame stays calm: a plain soft background, no faces or hands there.

sources.title: Language Development: 1 Year Olds
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (from Caring for Your Baby and Young Child, 2009)
sources.quote: Early in the second year, your toddler will suddenly seem to understand everything you say. ... Most toddlers master at least fifty spoken words by the end of the second year and can put two words together to form a short sentence, although there are differences among children. ... By all means, don’t ridicule his language mistakes. Give him as much time as he needs to finish what he wants to say without hurrying, and then answer with a correct pronunciation of the word (“That’s right, it’s a ball!”). ... He might point and say “ball”—his way of telling you he wants you to roll him the ball.
sources.supports: Toddlers seem to understand more than they say, differences among children, giving time, answering with the correct word without ridicule, and pointing with a single word as an early sentence. An American Academy of Pediatrics page (2009) applied to Israeli families as general advice.

sources.title: First words and little sentences: 1 to 2 years
sources.quote: Chatting about your daily routine, like getting dressed, is a great way for your child to hear the same words every day. ... Look at picture books together ... give your child time to point things out and talk about what they can see ... Name objects and offer your child choices, for example, "Do you want an apple or an orange?". ... Explore fun songs and rhymes with actions and props. Singing together is a great way to connect! ... Remember, children learn to talk at different ages. If you are worried, speak to your health visitor or nursery key worker
sources.supports: Talking through routines such as getting dressed, picture books and time to point, offering choices, songs with actions, and that children learn to talk at different ages. An NHS page for English families applied to Israeli families as general advice.
